A geological survey of your codebase.

How it works

Five layers, each made by a program from the one below.

Nothing in the stack is written by a model.

Run it twice on the same commit and every layer comes out byte for byte the same.

Explanation

Solid where the code proves it. Dashed where it doesn’t.

On Faultline’s own code

  • 29,747 claims.
  • 28,362 solid.
  • 1,385 dashed.

Drawn on the map at the top: 450 boxes with a “?”, 489 dashed roads.

Accurately located
Inferred
???In doubt

Geologists have drawn faults this way for over a century: a solid line where the fault is accurately located, a dashed line where it is inferred, a question mark where its existence is in doubt. A map that hides the difference is worse than no map.

Faultline draws the same way. A box or road is solid when a type checker or the flow graph decided it. It is dashed with a “?” when the tool only matched a name, or can’t see the caller. Open it and the panel says why.

  • Decision: the road out is labelled with its condition

  • Loop: with what limits it, when the code shows that

  • Wait: something else has to wake it

  • Store or send: a place that writes, deletes or calls out

  • Ending: success, failure, refusal, or neutral

  • Road: what leads to what

  • Road, dashed: not confident, and the panel says why

  • Box with "?": the tool wrote a label, but the evidence is thinner than the words

Line styles: Soller et al., USGS Open-File Report 02-370 (citing a 1920 plate); FGDC-STD-013-2006.

Two readers

One map, two readers.

People get one HTML file to zoom, hover and walk. Agents get the same map as short text, with a token cap on every answer. Same box, same id, so you can hand your agent the exact spot you mean.

The six commands an agent can call, what each answers, and the most tokens each may spend
CommandAnswersCap, tokens
briefwhat the code is, what was read and what's open1200
wherewhich box, its roads in and out600
breaksthe ranked questions800
patha route the roads allow, with its conditions400
impactwhat's downstream, which endings are reachable500
statuswhat was read, whether the page matches the map200

Also served over MCP: faultline mcp.

The whole thing, then one line

From the whole system to one line, without losing your place.

The whole system. 24 stages, 7,633 boxes, one file.

The question

When this fails, who hears about it?

Most of what goes wrong in production doesn’t crash. It fails quietly, somewhere nobody is looking. So at every failure and refusal in the code, Faultline asks who finds out: a person, the calling code, a log, or nobody.

When the code doesn’t say, the page says “not known from the code” and leaves it open. It doesn’t guess.

A candidate is a question, not a bug. Nothing here was run, and many will turn out to be fine.

We put that question to three real systems, up to 124,000 lines. Then a separate checker tried to knock down what it surfaced: 97 verdicts, 65 held, 26 partly held, 4 were wrong, 2 stayed unclear. Read, not run, apart from two tiny scripts.

Programs draw

Programs draw. The agent never does.

An agent that draws your map can invent a road that isn’t there, and you would never know. So the map is made with no model at all: no key, no network, nothing to write by hand.

An agent helps in two places only. It can answer the questions the tool flagged, citing a line that the tool re-reads. And it can write a story on top: what the code is for, which the code can’t say. Every word stays marked as words.

What we measured, including what didn't work.

The same drawing rule, on our own results

  • Solid. Recorded in full, and a script checks it.
  • Dashed. One run, one reader, or a different setup.
Field notes: each result, how it was measured, and what it does not show
Entry AResult BHow it was measured CWhat it doesn't show
1Solid mark: recorded in full and checked by a script. Same commit, same bytes. All 7 main files, the page included, are byte for byte identical across two runs. 5 of 1,400 files differ, and they are timing logs. Two runs of faultline map on BullMQ at commit a0ec9c0, into two empty folders, 25 seconds each. Then a hash of every main file and a byte comparison of every file. A fresh run also matches the tool map on this page. It holds for the same tool versions and the same Python environment. Change either and the bytes can change. It shows the drawing repeats, not that it is right. One Windows 10 PC.
2Dashed mark: one run, one reader, or a different setup. Blind readers. Tool map 18 of 24, story map 22 of 24. Readers were given only the page and twelve tasks. One reader per page. One reader per page, so it cannot separate the page from the reader. It says nothing about a reader who also has the code open.
3Dashed mark: one run, one reader, or a different setup. The attacker. 129 boxes and roads read against the source, across three systems. 0 false. Upper bound 2.3%. Hand-read by an attacker trying to find a false one, plus scripts over every map. The scripts did find false roads: six, on one large system, all through a finally block inside a loop. Some words on top of the map were wrong too. Treat switch defaults and error-handler wording as leads, not facts.
4Dashed mark: one run, one reader, or a different setup. A separate checker tried to knock down what the question surfaced. 97 verdicts: 65 held, 26 partly held, 4 were wrong, 2 stayed unclear. We put the question to three real systems, up to 124,000 lines. The checker read the code. Nothing was run, apart from two tiny scripts. It was run on hand-written maps, not on the tool maps. A candidate that held is a question that survived, not a failure seen in production.
5Dashed mark: one run, one reader, or a different setup. Agents, with and without the map. Orientation on a large system took about half the tokens (57k vs 115k). Pointed questions: no real difference. Known defects by symptom: no faster at all. The same tasks given to an agent with the map and without it. One run per question. One run per question, so no spread. The map doesn't find bugs. Asking who hears does.
6Dashed mark: one run, one reader, or a different setup. The story check can't read words. 36 of 123 planted fakes still read clean. Fake lines were planted in a story layer, then the story check was run over it. It proves two lines are joined, nothing about what the words claim. The page says what it can't see.
7Dashed mark: one run, one reader, or a different setup. The exam. 75 facts about BullMQ, answered with only the map's text commands. Tool map 32. Story map 61. One marker, answers unlabelled, checked against the source. One agent per map. The text commands were improved after this exam and not re-tested. Words from an agent still carry a lot: the map alone gets about half as far.

What this map can't tell you.

  • It reads code. It doesn't run it. A candidate is a shape worth a question.

  • It can't read intent. It doesn't know what matters, what success means, or why a retry exists. That is what the story layer is for.

  • Callbacks, decorators and dynamic names are flagged, not guessed. 1,204 calls on BullMQ couldn't be followed, and the page says so.

  • Stages are groups of folders, not steps. The tool claims no running order.

  • Very large code doesn't get a chart for every function. The page stays under 16 MB, and the rest are outlines.

  • Tested on: Windows 10, Node 24, Python 3.13. Treat anything else as unknown, and tell us.

Not this

  • It isn't a linter: it doesn't tell you what to change.
  • It isn't a call graph: roads carry conditions, and endings have outcomes.
  • It isn't a model checker: a checker proves what breaks inside a small model, and this shows where that break sits in the whole system, what leads there, and what nobody has checked. They work well together.

A larger test

See it on a large codebase.

BullMQ is an open source job queue: about 30,000 lines of TypeScript and Lua. We mapped it both ways, by programs alone and with an agent writing the story on top, and gave each page to a blind reader. Same code, side by side, including what didn’t work.

BullMQ, surveyed

Point it at your code.

npx github:EmergentKnowledgeGroup/FaultlineByEKG map --source .

Then open .faultline/dist/atlas.html. One file. No server, no network. Your code is only read.

Python? Run faultline setup once first: it fetches a pinned type checker and checks its hash. TypeScript, JavaScript and Lua come with the install. Node 24 or newer.

For your agent: skills/faultline/SKILL.md, or faultline mcp.
